drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: Your opponent was after your queen: their rook on d1 is looking straight down the d-file at your queen on d3. Qxa3 gets the queen out of danger, but it only wins a pawn on the rim, and after their queen takes f5 you're trading pawns while their rooks come alive, costing you about two pawns of your +7.3 advantage. Qxd1 is the stronger answer, because your queen takes the rook that was attacking it. After Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1 you lose your queen and the f7 bishop but win back their queen and the rook, so you come out a rook for a bishop ahead. The principle: when a rook attacks your queen, check first whether the queen can take that rook.

drills.coachNote: Their idea was Nxh4, winning your bishop outright, since the knight on f3 covers h4. Bf6 saves the piece, but it's a passive retreat that lets the knight jump to g5 and force a trade, and you give up roughly 1.6 pawns of your +6.8 edge. Bxf2+ is sharper: the bishop takes the f2 pawn with check, and after Kh1 Bf7 Qg5 Bxe1 Rxe1 you've collected a pawn and a rook for your bishop. The principle: when a piece is attacked, first look for a capture or check that wins material before you simply run away.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop on d3 is the target, attacked by the knight on b4 and the bishop on g6 with only your queen on d1 holding it. Qb3 pulls the queen off that defence to hit the knight on b4, but Bxd3 wins the bishop, and the Nxa7 Kxa7 Qxb4 sequence just swaps knights and grabs a pawn. You were already at +0.7, and this drops about four pawns. Rc7 is the stronger move: the rook hits their queen on d7 with tempo, and your knight on b5 guards c7, so the initiative stays with you. The principle: before you move a defender, check what it's guarding, because the piece it protects is the one that falls.

drills.coachNote: Black's bishop on d6 is lined up on your bishop on f4, and trading there is their plan. Nb5 is the stronger reply: the knight from c3 adds a second attacker to d6, where their queen is the only defender, and after Bxf4 Nxa7+ you pick up a pawn with check. drills.coachNote: White's only real hope was to untangle with Nd2 and bring a defender toward the king, and Rxb2 hands over that time for a pawn. Qg2 was mate in one: the queen slides from c6 along c6-d5-e4-f3-g2, and your rook on f2 defends it so Kxg2 is impossible. You were at +20, so the pawn meant nothing and the mate meant everything, and after Nd2 Qc2 Rh2 Qxd3 the game becomes a long chase when it could have ended on the spot. Before taking anything, check the enemy king's escape squares, because here only g2 mattered.

drills.coachNote: Black wants its king to reach f7 and come forward, and the square you pick decides how well your e-pawn can advance. Kf4 looks natural, but Kf7 followed by e4 Ke7 Ke3 is the line the engine punishes, costing about ten pawns of eval. Kf3 keeps your king on the f-file, where it can step to e3 once the pawn push goes in. In king-and-pawn endings, put the king on the square that supports the pawn push and keeps the opposing king out, rather than the square that just looks central.

drills.coachNote: Black wants his king to walk through e7 toward d6, where it would press your c6 pawn, which nothing defends. Bb3 spends the tempo your king needed: after Ke7 your king has to go to c4, and Black returns with Kf7, so you've lost time while sitting almost twenty pawns up. Ba2 reaches the same long diagonal but gets your king moving at once, and Ke7 Kc4 Ke8 Kb5 Kd8 has your king arriving on b5 to press the a5 and b6 pawns. The principle is that in a king race you count tempi, and the move that brings your king closer to the target beats one that just looks tidy.

You were about five and a half pawns up, and this move throws the whole game away in one go. Qd7+ comes first, a check that pushes the king to f6, and then O-O-O puts a rook on d1 so the knight has a second defender. drills.coachNote: The rook on h5 is aiming at your bishop on e5 along the fifth rank, so Rxe5 is what's coming. Qd4 does guard the bishop, but it gives Black the tempo to untangle with Qd7, and you've handed back about five pawns of a six-pawn edge. Qg6+ is the stronger idea: it checks along the g6-e8 diagonal and attacks the rook on h5 at the same time. After Kd7 the Qxh5 wins the rook while your queen stays active, and Kc6 Nd4+ keeps the king under fire. The principle is to look for checks that also hit a second piece, because a check that forks is the cleanest gain on the board.

drills.coachNote: The b-file is the only route your rook has to stop that pawn from queening. Rc4+ looks forcing, but Kd5 hits the rook right away, and after Rc3 b7 Rb3 your rook is a step behind the pawn, which is how about four pawns of a seven-pawn edge slipped away. Rc1 keeps the rook on the first rank, where it can reach b1 the moment the pawn advances. The line Rc1 b7 Re1+ Kd5 Rb1 puts the rook on the b-file as a blockade, and Rc6 then starts picking at the a6 pawn. The principle is that a check is only good if the king's reply doesn't hit your rook, so look at where the king goes before you give it.

Ra7 stays on the seventh rank, covers b7 directly, and attacks the a6 pawn, which only Re6 defends along the sixth rank. The principle is to ask what your rook is guarding before you move it, since the move that looks safe often removes the only defender of a square.

Qh7 is the answer, because it offers a queen trade on h7 and removes the queen that's doing the damage. After Qxh7+ Kxh7 the attack on f8 is gone, and the back-rank danger is over. The principle is to check, before any move, which of your back-rank pieces depends on a rook you're about to move.

After Qxf6+ Rg7 Qxc6 your queen gets to g6 and stays in the fight, but you've traded a rook for a bishop and lost the c6 bishop too. Nbd7 is the answer, because it backs up your f6 knight and keeps the knight trade from working for White. The line Rd1 Re8 Ne4 Qxd2 Nxd2 shows the queens coming off on your terms.
